short: A deep Transformer neural network trained on massive text corpora to understand, reason over, and generate human language.
eli5: An AI that read a library of millions of books and websites so it can predict helpful, fluent answers to almost any prompt.
example: Models that write code, summarize research papers, and hold multi-turn conversations.

short: The fundamental text unit—typically a word, subword, or punctuation mark—that an LLM reads and predicts one step at a time.
eli5: A single puzzle piece of language: roughly three-quarters of an English word on average.
example: The word 'chatbots' splitting into two tokens: 'chat' (ID 1532) and 'bots' (ID 28411).

short: A dense list of numbers representing the semantic meaning of a token, sentence, or image in continuous vector space.
eli5: Translating an idea into GPS coordinates in 'meaning space' so related concepts live in the same neighborhood.
example: Mapping a user support ticket to a 1,536-number vector to find matching help articles.

short: A mechanism allowing a model to dynamically weight which parts of an input sequence are most relevant when producing each output.
eli5: Using a spotlight while reading so your eyes jump back to the exact earlier word that clarifies a pronoun like 'it'.
example: Connecting 'it' strongly to 'battery' rather than 'phone' in 'The phone died because it was old'.

short: An attention layer where every token in a sequence compares itself with every other token in the same sequence using Queries, Keys, and Values.
eli5: Everyone in a room raising a question ('Query'), waving an introduction tag ('Key'), and sharing notes ('Value') with the best matches.
example: Resolving coreference and verb agreement simultaneously across a 4,000-token paragraph.

short: Running several independent self-attention heads in parallel so the model can track grammar, meaning, and long-range links simultaneously.
eli5: Having multiple readers scan the same page at once—one tracking pronouns, one tracking tone, and one tracking dates.
example: A 32-head Transformer layer attending to both adjacent punctuation and topic words pages earlier.

short: A parallel neural architecture built from stacked self-attention and feed-forward blocks that powers modern LLMs and multimodal AI.
eli5: An assembly line of spotlights that looks at all words in a sentence at once instead of plodding through one word at a time.
example: The 2017 'Attention Is All You Need' architecture behind modern frontier language and vision models.

short: Mathematical signals added to token embeddings or attention rotations (like RoPE) so a parallel Transformer knows word order.
eli5: Stamping seat numbers onto every word so the model still knows who arrived first even though it reads everyone together.
example: Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) encoding relative distances between tokens in long contexts.

short: The maximum number of tokens an LLM can hold in working memory at once across both prompt and generated output.
eli5: The size of the model's desk—everything it needs to read and write must fit on that desk at the same time.
example: Passing a 100-page PDF plus a question into a model with a 128k-token context limit.

short: The initial large-scale training phase where an LLM learns language, facts, and patterns via self-supervised next-token prediction.
eli5: Years of general schooling where the model reads everything to learn how the world and language fit together.
example: Training a base model on trillions of web, book, and code tokens before assistant tuning.

short: Further training a pretrained model on smaller, specialized, or instruction-formatted datasets to tailor its behavior or domain skill.
eli5: Sending a college graduate to medical school or culinary training to master one specialized craft.
example: Adapting a general base model on medical Q&A transcripts or structured JSON output examples.

short: A decoding parameter that scales output logits before softmax, balancing predictable accuracy (low) against creative variety (high).
eli5: A randomness dial: near zero picks the safest obvious word, while turning it up encourages surprising word choices.
example: Setting temperature to 0.1 for SQL generation and 0.8 for brainstorming story titles.
